# How to Stop Sending Job Applicants to 404 Pages

In recent posts, we’ve addressed common reasons web scrapes stop working and best practices for ensuring the scrapes fueling your job board are up and running. Here, we’ll dive deeper into one specific problem many job boards have: sending applicants to 404 pages – i.e., linking from a job posting to a URL that cannot be found.

For job boards, sending applicants to 404 pages not only prevents open jobs from getting filled, it also costs you money if you’re buying traffic and costs your customers if you’re charging them via a CPC model. For applicants, 404 pages are a terrible experience.

Here’s a look at three common reasons job listings link to 404 pages and two ways you can keep from sending interested candidates to broken links.

## Background: 3 Reasons Job Posts Link to 404 Pages

Job scrapes can break for many reasons, but the most common reasons we see that a listing links to a 404 page are these:


- The scraped URL changes, moves, or is taken down : This can happen for any number of reasons: the job was filled and the listing taken down, the job was edited and reposted at a new URL, the listing company redesigned its website, and so on. When any of these happens, the URL included in the original scrape now returns a 404 error. This is the most common reason we see a 404 error.

- The scraped URL contains session ID parameters : In other words, when the scrape was created, the scraped “apply” link included parameters unique to that session, meaning that that URL wouldn’t work later when others clicked it.

- The scraped URL contains other parameters : Companies that list job openings may tag individual listing pages with any number of parameters – and change them for many reasons. E.g., if they’re using URL parameters to track applicants by month, they’ll update those parameters when a new month starts. When they do, the old URL may return a 404 error.


In all these cases, a user clicks an “apply now” or similar button and ultimately discovers that there’s no job on the other end. Our research indicates that candidates drop off the site at that point.

So how big a problem is this for job boards?

We’ve found that about two percent of jobs change every day : they close, they get edited, the tracking parameters used in their URLs get updated, etc. In a week, that means 10 percent of the links you’re sending applicants to might not work.

So if you’re not doing anything to monitor and correct 404 links in job postings and you’re sending CPC traffic to posts, you can safely assume you’re wasting about 10 percent of that CPC budget .

Now let’s look at two ways to avoid sending traffic to 404 pages.

## Option 1: Prevent 404 Errors by Monitoring Scrapes

Monitoring your scrapes is one way to prevent the expensive problem of sending traffic to 404 pages. It’s difficult – in many cases impossible – to monitor the scrapes manually.

As we’ve noted in previous blog posts, monitoring amounts to about 80 percent of the work of managing web scrapes. What’s more, while the initial setup of a scrape is a process that has a clear end, monitoring is ongoing: as long as the scrape is live, you have to monitor it to ensure it’s returning valid results. Even with automatic monitoring, someone must review the error messages and correct the errors to avoid sending candidates to 404 pages.

Think of the analogy of doing a big landscaping project in your yard. The initial work is considerable: you have to plan the space, dig, plant, mulch, and so on. But that’s just the beginning; if you want your yard to look good for the long term, you have to maintain it day after day. If you don’t do any maintenance work, such as daily watering or periodic weeding, your yard will revert to its natural state. This is because of the fundamental process of entropy: left unchecked, disorder increases over time.

In the world of web scrapes, something similar happens: we’ve found that, in about six months, almost every source needs some kind of correction. But if you’re monitoring your scrapes on a regular basis, you can make those corrections as things break so that your job board is continually serving valid links and you never have an unwieldy maintenance project on your hands.

## Option 2: Prevent 404 Errors via UTM Logistics

UTM logistics is a relatively new discipline in the world of digital marketing. It involves monitoring, analyzing, and reporting on performance based on UTM parameters. If you’re using UTM parameters to track job listings, you may be able to identify and fix 404 errors as part of your UTM logistics work.

For example, a job board advertising positions on Facebook might tag its Facebook apply links with a specific UTM parameter. The job board might then send those leads to an employer paying for a listing with additional UTM parameters. When the employer tracks apply rates from various sources (as defined by UTM parameters), it can easily see trends that signal a potential 404 link: for example, if zero percent of leads from one source are completing an application, that’s a signal that something may be wrong with the listing and that they should check it.

It’s worth noting that, in this context, UTM logistics amounts to a different form of monitoring job listings. It’s not necessarily easier or less labor-intensive than the types of monitoring we do for a standard listing, but if your organization is already engaging in UTM logistics, this may be the simplest way to monitor job postings for 404 errors.

## How Often Should You Monitor Job Scrapes?

Whether you’re doing dedicated monitoring or modifying UTM logistics efforts to keep an eye on your job scrapes, daily monitoring is ideal for most scenarios.

At this rate, you’re ensuring that no broken links (or other problems) are live for more than 24 hours, which means you’re proactively limiting the problems they might cause (including wasted spend on CPC campaigns).

Daily monitoring also limits the load required to pull and process data.

In some cases, though, having near real-time accuracy matters to job boards. Those situations call for more frequent monitoring. We’ve found that four times per day is adequate to accommodate most of these situations, though it is possible to monitor much more frequently. The more often you monitor, the greater the load on your servers and other technology.

One way to minimize that load is to outsource scrape maintenance , though you can expect to pay a premium if you want monitoring carried out more frequently than daily.

## Weed Out 404 Pages with Ongoing Maintenance

Sending job applicants to 404 pages is expensive. The solution is straightforward, but requires investment of a different kind: the time and energy of developers tasked with monitoring scrapes on an ongoing basis, plus the processing power to handle ongoing monitoring efforts.

If you’d like to stop losing money and / or stop creating poor visitor experiences by sending applicants to 404 pages but you don’t have the resources to staff a team of developers dedicated to monitoring, get in touch . We can handle the work of building and monitoring your scrapes, with greater accuracy and for less money than what you’d be able to do in house.

# Finding a job with web scraping







Por Renne Rocha | February 07, 2025
| 8 minutos




Web Scraping

Scrapy

Playwright













A few months ago I was looking for a new job. This means spending hours browsing LinkedIn and/or job boards and drowning into outdated ads or positions that weren’t looking for someone with my skills.

After applying for some of these jobs, I realized that many companies around the world use recruitment platforms such as greenhouse.io and lever.co to receive applications. However, it is not possible through these platforms to search directly for the current openings. I was still relying on Linkedin ads or being lucky to see some of them being announced by a recruiter in some social network.

Most search engines allow us to search for keywords by limiting the results only within a specific domain. Usually adding site: together with our search terms will return only results in this domain. So if I search for the keywords related to the positions I want limiting my results to the recruitment platforms that I know would give me a list of job postings that probably I wouldn’t find easily and more likely to be still accepting applicants.

If I also gather information inside each job posting, I can filter them so I can apply only in the ones that are looking for someone with my skills, experience and location.

I didn’t want to do it manually, and given that I have a good experience with web scraping I decided to implement something that would help me to collect all this data.

## Tools and Libraries

### Scrapy

Scrapy is my default choice when performing web scraping projects. It is a simple and extensible framework that allows
me to start to gather data from websites very quickly but powerful
enough if I want to expand and build a more robust project.

### Playwright

Although it is possible to scrape JavaScript-heavy websites without requiring a real browser to render the content, I decided to use Playwright , a tool for testing web applications that automate browser interactions but it also can be used in web scraping tasks. It also helps me to avoid beingh easily identified as a bot and being blocked to scrape the data.

### scrapy-playwright

scrapy-playwright is a plugin that makes easier to integrate Playwright and make it to adhere to the regular Scrapy workflow.

## Development

### Preparing our environment

Project is a common Python project developed inside a virtualenv.

mkdir job_search
cd job_search
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install scrapy scrapy-playwright
Copy

Then create a Scrapy project and configure scrapy-playwright following the installation and activation instructions available in the extension documentation.

scrapy startproject postings
cd postings
Copy

# postings/settings.py
# (...)

# Add the following to the existing file
DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS = {
"http" : "scrapy_playwright.handler.ScrapyPlaywrightDownloadHandler" ,
"https" : "scrapy_playwright.handler.ScrapyPlaywrightDownloadHandler" ,
}
Copy

### Gathering URL of job postings

In Scrapy terminology, a Spider is a class which we define how to scrape and crawl information from a certain site. So let’s create one Spider to perform a search in DuckDuckGo passing as search parameters: (1) the domain we want the results and (2) keywords we want to be inside the results (so we can filter only the job postings of the technology/position we are interested).

# postings/spiders/duckduckgo.py
import itertools
from urllib.parse import urlparse
import scrapy
import w3lib.url

class DuckDuckGoSpider (scrapy . Spider):
name = "duckduckgo"
allowed_domains = [ "duckduckgo.com" ]

def start_requests (self):
...

def parse (self, response, keyword):
...
Copy

Inside start_request method, we schedule the initial requests sending search queries to DuckDuckGo passing domains and keywords we are interested.

Adding meta={"playwright": True} to the request ensures that a real browser (managed by playwright and scrapy-playwright) will be used. This will help us not to be easily identified as a bot (and blocked). Using a real browser (instead of sending plain requests only) will make our spider to be slower. Given that this spider will not be running frequently, we can accept the slowness of opening a real browser and perform the operations on it.

We also add cb_kwargs as a way to send some metadata to the request that will be used later to add extra information in the data returned.

def start_requests (self):
keywords = [ "python" , "django" , "flask" , "fastapi" ]
domains = [ "jobs.lever.co" , "boards.greenhouse.io" ]

for domain, keyword in itertools . product(domains, keywords):
yield scrapy . Request(
f "https://duckduckgo.com/?q=site%3A { domain } + { keyword } " ,
meta = { "playwright" : True },
cb_kwargs = { "keyword" : keyword},
)
Copy

Next step is to implement parse method that will get the response from DuckDuckGo and gather the URLs of the job postings.

def parse (self, response, keyword):
for url in response . css( "a::attr(href)" ) . getall():
parsed_url = urlparse(url)
if parsed_url . netloc not in [ "jobs.lever.co" , "boards.greenhouse.io" ]:
# Ignore results not in the domains we are interested
continue

company_name = parsed_url . path . split( "/" )[ 1 ]

yield {
"company" : company_name,
"job_posting_url" : url,
"keyword" : keyword,
}
Copy

Running the Spider and exporting the results into a CSV file.

scrapy crawl duckduckgo -o job_postings.csv
Copy

And now we have an initial version of our spider and we are able to collect links of job postings that matches our search keywords.

### Handling page pagination

This initial run of the spider probably will return just a few results (~10). Performing this search manually, we will notice that what we got until now is just the first page of the results. Looking at DuckDuckGo results page, we can notice in the bottom the following button that when clicked will load more results.

scrapy-playwright (and playwright ) allows us to perform actions on pages such filling forms or clicking elements, so we can change our spider that when we perform the search, we will click in More Results button until we can’t find it in the page anymore (indicating that we don’t have more hidden results to be shown).

First we create our function that will get the page, and click the button as many times as needed. When the button is not visible anymore (we reach our maximum number of results), PlaywrightTimeoutError is raised stopping the interactions with the page and releasing it to be parsed.

# postings/spiders/duckduckgo.py
from playwright.async_api import TimeoutError as PlaywrightTimeoutError


async def more_results (page):
while True :
try :
await page . locator(selector = "#more-results" ) . click()
except PlaywrightTimeoutError:
break
return page . url
Copy

Then we add playwright_page_methods with the list of methods that we want to be called on the page.

# postings/spiders/duckduckgo.py

class DuckDuckGoSpider (scrapy . Spider):
# (...)

def start_requests (self):
keywords = [ "python" , "django" , "flask" , "fastapi" ]
domains = [ "jobs.lever.co" , "boards.greenhouse.io" ]

for domain, keyword in itertools . product(domains, keywords):
yield scrapy . Request(
f "https://duckduckgo.com/?q=site%3A { domain } + { keyword } " ,
meta = {
"playwright" : True ,
"playwright_page_methods" : [
PageMethod(more_results),
],
},
cb_kwargs = { "keyword" : keyword},
)
Copy

Running the Spider again, we will get all the results.

### Removing duplicated results

After running the Spider, we will notice that some URLs are duplicated. One of the reasons is that more than one search keyword can return the same job posting result (we would expect a Django job posting also having Python keyword inside it).

To drop the duplicated values, we can create an Item Pipeline that will check, for each job posting returned whether it was returned before or not.

An item pipeline is a simple class that implements process_item method that receives items returned by the Spider, perform some processing on the item and then return it or drop it. When enabled all items returned by DuckDuckGoSpider will pass through it.

A seen_urls set is defined, so we can check if that particular URL was already returned (and then we can skip it) or if it is a new URL.

# postings/pipelines.py
from scrapy.exceptions import DropItem


class JobPostingDuplicatesPipeline :
seen_urls = set()

def process_item (self, item, spider):
if item[ "job_posting_url" ] in self . seen_urls:
# We drop items which the URL was already returned before
raise DropItem( "Already returned" )

# Add the URL to the set when it was processed for the first time
self . seen_urls . add(item[ "job_posting_url" ])

yield item
Copy

We need to enable this pipeline in our project.

# postings/settings.py
# (...)

ITEM_PIPELINES = {
"postings.pipelines.JobPostingDuplicatesPipeline" : 300 ,
}
Copy

We can run again the Spider, exporting the results into a CSV file. This time, we will have only unique job posting URLs.

scrapy crawl duckduckgo -o job_postings.csv
Copy

### Possible improvements

This is the starting point of our job search. It was useful to me because it returned some companies that I have never heard about it, looking for professionals with the skills that I have. Certainly this narrowed more my options and helped me to apply to positions that made more sense to me.

A possible improvement would be create a specific spider for each recruitment platform to parse the content of the job postings. This would allow us to filter even more our data. For example, we can check for specific benefits or other keywords that would be useful for us to decide to apply or not to the job.

### Summary

Here we have the complete code:

# postings/pipelines.py
import itertools
from urllib.parse import urlparse

import scrapy
import w3lib.url
from playwright.async_api import TimeoutError as PlaywrightTimeoutError
from scrapy_playwright.page import PageMethod


async def more_results (page):
while True :
try :
await page . locator(selector = "#more-results" ) . click()
except PlaywrightTimeoutError:
break
return page . url


class DuckDuckGoSpider (scrapy . Spider):

def start_requests (self):
keywords = [ "python" , "django" , "flask" , "fastapi" ]
domains = [ "jobs.lever.co" , "boards.greenhouse.io" ]

for domain, keyword in itertools . product(domains, keywords):
yield scrapy . Request(
f "https://duckduckgo.com/?q=site%3A { domain } + { keyword } " ,
meta = {
"playwright" : True ,
"playwright_page_methods" : [
PageMethod(more_results),
],
},
cb_kwargs = { "keyword" : keyword},
)

def parse (self, response, keyword):
for url in response . css( "a::attr(href)" ) . getall():
parsed_url = urlparse(url)
if parsed_url . netloc not in [ "jobs.lever.co" , "boards.greenhouse.io" ]:
# Ignore results not in the domains we are interested
continue

company_name = parsed_url . path . split( "/" )[ 1 ]

yield {
"company" : company_name,
"job_posting_url" : url,
"keyword" : keyword,
}
Copy

# postings/settings.py
# (...)

# Add the following to the existing file
DOWNLOAD_HANDLERS = {
"http" : "scrapy_playwright.handler.ScrapyPlaywrightDownloadHandler" ,
"https" : "scrapy_playwright.handler.ScrapyPlaywrightDownloadHandler" ,
}

ITEM_PIPELINES = {
"postings.pipelines.JobPostingDuplicatesPipeline" : 300 ,
}
Copy

class JobPostingDuplicatesPipeline :
seen_urls = set()

def process_item (self, item, spider):
if item[ "job_posting_url" ] in self . seen_urls:
# We drop items which the URL was already returned before
raise DropItem( "Already returned" )

# Add the URL to the set when it was processed for the first time
self . seen_urls . add(item[ "job_posting_url" ])

yield item
Copy

Good luck with your job hunt!

# Best Practice for Removing Expired Job Listings



Hi Google Team,



I run a job board where job listings expire frequently. I want to remove these pages properly to avoid SEO issues. Since Webflow doesn’t support 410 status codes, what’s the best approach? Should I:

- Use  Google Search Console’s Removal Tool  each time?
- Rely on  natural deindexing  after deletion?
- Use  301 redirects  to job category pages (but too many redirects could be bad)?
- Keep the page live & mark the job as expired with “Noindex” (which Webflow doesn’t support natively)?


What’s the best way to handle this without harming SEO?



Thanks

Ah ok!

The API can be used to notify Google of URls that have become 404

https://developers.google.com/search/apis/indexing-api/v3/quickstart

- Remove a URL : After you delete a page from your servers, notify Google so that we can remove the page from our index and so that we don't attempt to crawl the URL again.


Honestly, I dont know if the URL Removals function actull blocks a job/page from appearing in Job Results.

(its intended for blocking pages from organic web results, blocking in other results is less certain)



Note that with a block in place, Google can still recrawl and remove the page from index. It doesnt wait until the block expires for crawling.





Also would note, that Google treaks 410 same as 404, there is no real benefit of having 410.

... the generic 404 is fine, and works the same.

(would be very surpised if provider doesnt support 404s)

results.snippet: Job search aggregators solve this by scanning thousands of sources automatically, delivering every relevant opening in one searchable interface so you spend time applying instead of hunting. Free for job seekers with optional premium features, Indeed generates revenue through employer job postings and sponsored listings that appear prominently in search results. Glassdoor started as a company review and salary sharing site before adding job search functionality, creating a unique combination where you research employers while browsing openings. Yes, all major job aggregators including Careerjet, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, LinkedIn Jobs, Glassdoor, SimplyHired, Jooble, and LinkUp offer free job searching and application features for candidates. # 2025's Top 8 Best Job Search Aggregator Platforms



Visiting 47 different job boards daily just to find three relevant openings feels like a full-time job before you even have a job. Traditional job hunting means manually checking company websites, niche industry boards, recruiter portals, and general job sites—burning hours finding duplicate listings or outdated posts from positions filled months ago. Job search aggregators solve this by scanning thousands of sources automatically, delivering every relevant opening in one searchable interface so you spend time applying instead of hunting. Whether you're switching careers, relocating cities, or just tired of missing opportunities buried on obscure company pages, these platforms compress the entire internet's job market into single dashboards with smart filters, email alerts, and mobile apps keeping opportunities flowing wherever you are.


## Careerjet

Global job search engine aggregating 40+ million listings from 58,000+ sources across 90 countries daily.

Careerjet operates as a pure search engine model, scanning the web continuously to index job postings from company career pages, recruitment agency sites, and specialized job boards. The platform never hosts listings directly—clicking any job redirects you to the original posting, ensuring information accuracy and letting you apply through proper channels. This aggregation approach means you see opportunities others miss because they're scattered across thousands of smaller employer websites nobody visits individually.

The technology behind Careerjet uses smart agents running on networked computer clusters that identify and scan 58,000+ websites every single day. These automated crawlers detect new job postings regardless of where they're published, adding them to the searchable index within hours. The daily scanning ensures listings remain current rather than displaying ghost jobs that disappeared weeks ago but linger on slower-updating platforms.

Coverage spans 90+ countries with interfaces translated into 28 languages, making Careerjet genuinely international. You search for marketing roles in Toronto, engineering positions in Singapore, or remote opportunities from Spanish-speaking countries—all through localized interfaces displaying results in your preferred language. This global reach suits expatriates, international job seekers, and anyone exploring opportunities beyond their home country.

The straightforward interface prioritizes speed over complexity. Search by keywords, location, and company name without navigating elaborate filter menus. Results load quickly with essential details—job title, company, location, posting date—letting you scan dozens of opportunities rapidly. This simplicity appeals to users who want efficient job discovery without learning complicated platform features.

Account creation remains optional for basic searching. You browse millions of jobs, read full descriptions, and click through to applications without registering. Creating a free account unlocks email alerts delivering daily job matches, saved searches for repeated queries, and CV upload for faster applications. The no-registration-required approach eliminates barriers for casual browsers while rewarding active seekers with convenience features.

Mobile apps on iOS and Android provide full functionality on phones, letting you job hunt during commutes, lunch breaks, or whenever opportunities arise. Apply directly from your device without awkward desktop-only application processes. Send interesting jobs to yourself or friends via email, maintaining your job search momentum regardless of location.


## Indeed

Industry-dominant aggregator processing 10 job uploads every second with 176+ million monthly visitors.

Indeed claims the title of world's largest job site, and the numbers back it up—176.8 million monthly visits dwarf most competitors. The platform's massive scale results from aggressive aggregation pulling listings from countless sources combined with direct employer postings. This dual approach captures both obscure opportunities from small companies and major openings from Fortune 500 employers.

The sheer volume means you find multiple relevant listings for most search queries. Looking for "software developer" in Austin returns hundreds of results spanning startups, established tech companies, consulting firms, and remote positions. This abundance gives job seekers options rather than settling for the three opportunities a niche board might display.

Company pages provide employer insights beyond basic job descriptions. You see reviews from current and former employees, salary information submitted anonymously by workers, interview experiences from actual candidates, and photos of office environments. This transparency helps evaluate whether companies match your expectations before investing time in applications.

Free for job seekers with optional premium features, Indeed generates revenue through employer job postings and sponsored listings that appear prominently in search results. While this means some results get visibility through paid placement, the fundamental search and apply functionality costs nothing for candidates.

Resume upload and one-click apply streamline application processes. Upload your resume once, then apply to compatible positions with single clicks rather than filling out identical information repeatedly. The time savings compound when applying to dozens of roles, though customizing applications for top-choice positions still matters for success rates.

Job alerts via email or mobile push notifications keep you informed when new matching opportunities appear. Configure alerts for specific titles, companies, or locations, then let Indeed notify you immediately when relevant postings go live. This responsiveness helps you apply early when competition is lowest.


## ZipRecruiter

AI-powered matching engine distributing applications across 100+ job boards with smart mobile experience.

ZipRecruiter differentiates through artificial intelligence that actively matches candidates to relevant openings rather than waiting for manual searches. Upload your resume and the AI analyzes your skills, experience, and preferences to automatically surface job recommendations. The system continues learning from your actions—which jobs you view, apply to, or pass on—refining recommendations over time.

The platform distributes your profile across 100+ job boards simultaneously when you apply through ZipRecruiter. One application reaches hiring managers on multiple platforms, multiplying your exposure without duplicate effort. This network effect increases response rates compared to applying through single-board listings.

Employers using ZipRecruiter receive candidate matches too, meaning you might get "invited to apply" notifications for positions matching your background. These invitations indicate employer interest, potentially improving your odds versus cold applications where you're one of 300 anonymous candidates. The two-way matching creates more engaged interactions than traditional job boards.

The mobile app earns high marks for usability, letting you browse, apply, and communicate with employers entirely from your phone. Push notifications alert you about new matches immediately, letting you apply within minutes of jobs going live. The seamless mobile experience suits job seekers who can't constantly check desktop computers.

One-click apply functionality works across most listings, though some employers require extended applications on their own websites. When one-click works, the time savings are significant—applying to 20 jobs takes minutes instead of hours filling out repetitive forms.

Pricing remains free for job seekers with employers paying for access. The platform generates value for candidates through AI matching, multi-board distribution, and employer invitations without requiring payment or premium subscriptions.


## LinkedIn Jobs

Professional network combining job listings with direct recruiter access and 551+ million user connections.

LinkedIn transforms job searching from anonymous applications into relationship-based opportunities. The platform's 551.6 million monthly visits include professionals networking, recruiters sourcing candidates, and employers building brand presence. This ecosystem means job listings exist alongside the people who posted them, enabling direct contact that other platforms lack.

Easy Apply functionality lets you submit applications using your LinkedIn profile rather than uploading resumes to each company's system. One click sends your complete professional history, recommendations, and connection network to employers. The convenience encourages applying to more positions while maintaining quality since your profile represents your complete brand.

Networking capabilities distinguish LinkedIn from pure job boards. You see which connections work at companies where you're applying, message mutual contacts for referrals, follow hiring managers to understand their priorities, and engage with company content demonstrating your interest. These relationship-building activities often matter more than application volume.

Premium Career subscriptions ($39.99+ monthly) provide advantages including InMail credits for messaging recruiters directly without connection requests, salary insights showing what positions actually pay, and "applicant insights" revealing how your qualifications compare to other candidates. The features assist serious job seekers willing to invest in accelerated searches, though basic functionality remains free.

Job recommendations appear in your feed based on profile analysis, showing relevant opportunities without explicit searching. The passive discovery helps you learn about openings you wouldn't have thought to search for, potentially uncovering career pivots or companies outside your usual radar.

Company pages offer deep insights including employee counts, growth trajectories, recent news, and cultural values. You research potential employers thoroughly before applying, ensuring alignment with your career goals rather than blindly submitting to any opening.


## Glassdoor

Salary transparency platform combining job search with employee reviews and 27+ million monthly users.

Glassdoor started as a company review and salary sharing site before adding job search functionality, creating a unique combination where you research employers while browsing openings. The 27.7 million monthly visits reflect professionals valuing transparency about workplace culture, compensation, and interview processes before committing to applications.

Salary data stands as Glassdoor's signature feature. You see reported salaries for specific positions at specific companies, submitted anonymously by employees. This transparency helps evaluate whether opportunities match financial expectations before investing time in lengthy interview processes. For example, Microsoft's Glassdoor page contains salary data for 192,000 positions, providing comprehensive compensation insights.

Company reviews from current and former employees reveal workplace realities beyond polished employer branding. You read about management quality, work-life balance, career development opportunities, and reasons people leave. These honest assessments help avoid toxic environments or companies misaligned with your priorities.

Interview reviews describe actual interview questions, process length, and candidate experiences at thousands of companies. Preparing for interviews becomes easier when you know what to expect rather than guessing what hiring managers might ask.

Job search functionality aggregates listings from multiple sources, functioning similarly to Indeed but with Glassdoor's transparency layer added. You apply through the platform while simultaneously researching whether the employer deserves your effort based on employee feedback and salary data.

Account creation requires name, email, and password—Glassdoor asks users to contribute reviews or salary data to maintain the community-driven transparency model. Recent updates require identity verification for certain features, balancing anonymity with authenticity.


## SimplyHired

User-friendly aggregator owned by Indeed parent company with salary estimators and straightforward search.

SimplyHired aggregates job postings from job boards, company websites, and government employment portals into one searchable database. The platform's simplicity appeals to job seekers overwhelmed by feature-heavy competitors—straightforward searching without elaborate profile building or algorithm training.

Salary estimator tools provide compensation insights for various roles and locations. While not as comprehensive as Glassdoor's user-submitted data, the estimates help set realistic salary expectations when evaluating opportunities or negotiating offers. You see typical ranges for "marketing manager in Denver" or "software engineer in Seattle" alongside relevant job listings.

Free and premium posting options for employers mean the platform contains both sponsored listings and organic results. As a job seeker, you don't pay anything—all search and apply functionality remains completely free without premium tiers limiting core features.

Resume database features let you upload resumes for employer viewing, though this passive approach works best when combined with active application to specific postings. Employers searching SimplyHired's resume database might contact you about opportunities, adding another discovery channel.

The platform lacks the advanced features of competitors like ZipRecruiter's AI matching or LinkedIn's networking capabilities. This simplicity can be refreshing for users who just want to search jobs efficiently without learning complex systems or optimizing profiles.

Broad job listing database covers various industries, experience levels, and locations across the United States and internationally. You find entry-level positions, mid-career opportunities, and executive roles spanning every major employment category.


## Jooble

International aggregator operating in 70+ countries with AI-driven recommendations and multilingual support.

Jooble pulls job listings from company career pages, job boards, and staffing agencies across 70+ countries, creating genuinely global coverage. The international reach suits job seekers exploring opportunities in multiple countries or relocating internationally for work.

AI-driven job recommendations analyze your search patterns and clicked listings to surface increasingly relevant opportunities over time. The system learns your preferences without requiring elaborate profile setup—simply use the platform and recommendations improve automatically.

Filters for experience level, salary ranges, and employment type help narrow vast result sets to qualified matches. You exclude entry-level positions when seeking senior roles, hide full-time openings when seeking contract work, or filter by minimum salary requirements eliminating underpaid opportunities.

No registration requirement for basic searching removes barriers to quick job discovery. Browse millions of listings, read full descriptions, and click through to applications without creating accounts or submitting personal information. This frictionless approach suits casual browsers and privacy-conscious searchers.

User-friendly interface emphasizes clarity over complexity. Search results display essential information cleanly without overwhelming visual clutter. You scan dozens of opportunities quickly, clicking through to full details on interesting positions without navigating confusing layouts.

Job listings sometimes link to external sites with their own application processes rather than standardized Jooble applications. This means application experiences vary—some companies offer simple online forms while others require multi-step processes through their proprietary systems.


## LinkUp

Direct-from-employer aggregator eliminating duplicates and expired listings by sourcing only from company websites.

LinkUp takes a unique approach by exclusively indexing jobs directly from employer career pages rather than aggregating from third-party boards. This methodology eliminates duplicate listings, expired postings, and recruiter spam that plague broader aggregators pulling from multiple sources.

The direct sourcing ensures accuracy—every listed job exists on the employer's actual website at the time of display. You won't encounter ghost jobs that filled months ago but remain visible because aggregators haven't updated their databases. This accuracy saves time applying to real opportunities instead of submitting to positions that no longer exist.

Advanced job search filters include detailed criteria for refining results. You filter by posting date to see only recent openings, company size to target enterprises or startups, and other parameters helping identify optimal matches without sorting through thousands of irrelevant listings.

Higher accuracy in job listings comes from the elimination of third-party recruiter postings that sometimes misrepresent actual job details or represent the same position listed by multiple agencies. LinkUp's employer-direct approach means you see each opportunity once from the actual hiring company.

The platform provides clean, accurate job market data that works for both job seekers and market researchers studying employment trends. The data quality and timeliness exceed aggregators that tolerate duplicates and stale postings in exchange for higher listing counts.

Coverage includes 80,000+ companies across 195 countries, though the volume of listings is lower than mega-aggregators like Indeed. The trade-off between quantity and quality suits job seekers prioritizing accuracy over seeing every possible opening including duplicates and expired posts.


## FAQ

How do job aggregators differ from traditional job boards?

Job aggregators like Careerjet and Indeed scan thousands of sources automatically, compiling listings from company websites, recruitment agencies, and other job boards into one searchable database. Traditional job boards host jobs directly posted by employers paying to list openings. Aggregators provide broader coverage by pulling from multiple sources, while traditional boards offer only positions specifically posted to their platform. The aggregation approach means you see more opportunities from a single search, though some listings redirect to external sites for applications. Traditional boards typically offer more standardized application processes since everything stays within their system.

Are job aggregator platforms free to use for job seekers?

Yes, all major job aggregators including Careerjet, Indeed, ZipRecruiter, LinkedIn Jobs, Glassdoor, SimplyHired, Jooble, and LinkUp offer free job searching and application features for candidates. These platforms generate revenue from employers who pay for job postings, sponsored listings, resume database access, or applicant tracking features. Some platforms like LinkedIn offer optional premium subscriptions ($39.99+ monthly) providing advantages like direct recruiter messaging or enhanced insights, but core job search functionality remains free. You can browse millions of listings, apply to positions, and receive job alerts without paying anything.

How can I avoid applying to duplicate or expired job listings on aggregators?

Use platforms like LinkUp that source exclusively from employer websites, automatically eliminating duplicates since each company's careers page shows positions once. On broader aggregators, sort results by posting date to prioritize recent listings over old ones more likely to be filled. Check the original job posting URL—if multiple listings show the same company-hosted link, they're duplicates you can skip. Set up email alerts instead of browsing randomly; fresh listings arrive daily, reducing exposure to stale posts. When applying, verify the job still exists on the company's actual website before spending time on detailed applications. Cross-reference suspicious listings on employer sites to confirm legitimacy.


## Conclusion

Manually visiting dozens of job boards daily hoping to stumble across relevant openings wastes hours you could spend actually applying, networking, or improving skills. Job search aggregators automate the tedious discovery work by scanning thousands of sources continuously, delivering every relevant opportunity through single interfaces with smart filters, instant alerts, and mobile access keeping your search active 24/7 without constant manual checking. Careerjet excels specifically at global job discovery—scanning 58,000+ websites daily across 90 countries in 28 languages, making it ideal for international job seekers, expatriates exploring opportunities abroad, or anyone wanting comprehensive coverage spanning obscure company websites and major job boards mainstream platforms miss.
